Issued at 530 AM EST TUE NOV 17 2026

While the beginning of the long term forecast period continues to be 
defined by an amplified ridging pattern, change is now visible on 
the horizon. A series of shortwave troughs is progged to eject out 
of the Rockies and into the Greater Midwest between Thursday and 
Sunday. Models collectively keep the first disturbance well to the 
northwest of the JKL CWA. Its forecast trajectory into the Upper 
Midwest on Thursday means that there will be little to no 
immediately noticeable changes to the sensible weather forecast here 
in Eastern Kentucky. However, this impulse will work to suppress the 
antecedent mid/upper level ridging pattern. LREF mean 500mb 
geopotential heights drop from near the 98th percentile of model 
climatology on Wednesday evening to below the 75th percentile on 
Saturday afternoon. The ridge axis shifts from its initial overhead 
positioning to well to the east of the CWA in this same time frame. 
The initially anomalous strength of this feature will allow 
seasonably tranquil weather conditions to continue through the end 
of the work week, but increasingly effective warm/moist air 
advection around its western periphery will culminate in some 
noticeable forecast changes later this weekend. 

Subsidence in the immediate vicinity of the aforementioned ridge 
axis will help to keep a surface anticyclone in the vicinity of the 
forecast area through Friday night. Such a setup, along with the dry 
nature of the antecedent airmass, favors efficient diurnal cooling, 
heating, and mixing processes. Thus, the sensible weather forecast 
details in the latter stages of the work week will be governed by 
these radiational and mechanical cycles. As the sun sets, colder air 
will pool within the area's seasonally-shaded valleys. This should 
allow lower-elevation locales to decouple from the boundary layer at 
night. Modeled nocturnal radiation inversions and calm surface-
level winds further support this notion, so ridge-valley temperature 
splits have accordingly been added into the editable MinT grids. 
Expect valley fog and frost to develop in the valleys as 
temperatures dip into the 30s by morning. The warmer ridgetops 
should avoid these two mesoscale phenomena, as temperatures should 
remain closer to the 40 degree mark atop the inversion in these 
higher elevation locales. Once the sun comes up, ample solar 
insolation should yield above-normal highs in the 60s. A few 
locations could approach the 70 degree mark on Friday, but this is 
likely contingent upon diurnal mixing being deeper than what the 
baseline NBM guidance accounts for. Dewpoints should mix out towards 
afternoon minimums in the 30s under the ridging regime, but those 
values creep up towards the upper 30s on Friday. This marks the 
first symptom of the pattern change, and the airmass looks to 
moisten further this weekend. 

There has been a notable decrease in model spread surrounding the 
second shortwave troughing disturbance. The forecast guidance suite 
now collectively resolves a deeper moisture regime out ahead of it, 
which, in turn, has bolstered confidence in late period rain chances 
relative to this time yesterday. The flow aloft is now expected to 
turn southerly on Friday night, with moisture overrunning the 
antecedently dry low-level airmass. This yields an increase in cloud 
cover and some some slight chance PoPs on Saturday, but better rain 
chances arrive on Sunday. A brief period of deep southwesterly flow 
immediately ahead of the trough axis will advect a narrow tongue of 
moisture into the CWA ahead of an approaching cold front on Sunday 
afternoon. Ensemble mean PWATs surge towards the 1 inch within this 
time frame, and while these values are not record-breaking, they do 
rank above the 80th percentile of climatology for this traditionally-
dry time of year. They also mark a significant departure from the sub-
0.25 inch values observed at the start of the period, which will 
make it hard for Saturday's raindrops to actually reach the ground. 
Long story short, there looks to be relatively greater amounts of 
moisture in place on Sunday as the second shortwave arrives. That 
disturbance's trajectory has trended closer to the forecast area in 
recent model runs. So, combined with the presence of a better-
defined surface frontal boundary, there will also be relatively 
greater amounts of forcing in place. Sunday's rain chances have 
accordingly trended upward. There has been a general 10-20% increase 
in PoPs across the entire CWA on Sunday and Sunday night relative to 
what was in the forecast grids 24 hours ago. If the above model 
trends continue, those PoPs could increase beyond their current 20-
35% values. Given that last night's 00z LREF data now resolves up to 
a 50% chance of at least a tenth of an inch of rainfall across 
portions of the JKL CWA, such an increase appears likely. Flooding
